16452:
Hathor is not named in the Bible.

- **Sinai.** Egyptians mined turquoise at Serabit el-Khadim in south-western Sinai and built a large temple there to Hathor. Workers from Canaan left inscriptions in the earliest known alphabet, several addressed to Baalat, 'the Lady' — almost certainly Hathor. The location of biblical Mount Sinai is itself debated, but the region was not religiously empty when Israel passed through it.
- **The golden calf.** Some scholars suggest the calf at Sinai drew on Hathor's cow imagery as well as Apis's bull. The Hebrew word *egel* means a young bull, which fits Levantine bull iconography better. Debated.
- **Fifth plague.** As a cow goddess, Hathor is often listed in charts as a target of the plague on livestock (Exod 9:1-7). This pairing is traditional and debated (Exod 12:12; Num 33:4).

16486: Amun, 'the hidden one', was the god of Thebes who became king of the Egyptian gods during Egypt's empire. His vast temple at Karnak was one of the largest religious complexes ever built. Jeremiah names him directly — 'Amon of No' — and Nahum reminds Nineveh how Amun's city of Thebes fell.
16487: Amun was invisible and present everywhere, the hidden breath behind all things. When Theban kings drove out the Hyksos (c. 1550 BC) and built an empire, they credited Amun, merged him with the sun god as Amun-Ra, and showered his temple with plunder from Canaan and Nubia. The Amun priesthood became immensely rich. Pharaoh Akhenaten briefly suppressed Amun in favour of the sun disc Aten (c. 1350 BC), but Amun was restored under Tutankhamun ('living image of Amun').
16488:
Jeremiah's oracle against Egypt announces: 'Behold, I will punish Amon of No, and Pharaoh, and Egypt, with their gods and their kings' (Jer 46:25). The KJV translates *Amon mi-No* as 'the multitude of No', but modern translations recognise the god's name.

Nahum warns Nineveh: 'Are you better than No-Amon (populous No), that was situated among the rivers?' — yet she was carried into captivity and her infants dashed to pieces (Nah 3:8-10). This refers to the Assyrian sack of Thebes in 663 BC, which Nineveh itself had carried out. Ezekiel also predicts judgement on No (Ezek 30:14-16).

Amun's temple also records Israel's history from the Egyptian side: Shoshenq I, almost certainly the biblical Shishak, celebrated his campaign into Judah and Israel on a wall at Karnak (cf. 1 Kgs 14:25-26).

16529: Zeus was the king of the Greek gods, ruler of the sky and the thunderbolt; the Romans called him Jupiter. In Acts, the people of Lystra think Barnabas is Zeus and Paul is Hermes come down in human form, and the priest of Zeus tries to sacrifice oxen to them. Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes and insist they are only human.
16530:
Zeus was the youngest son of the Titan Cronus, who swallowed his children for fear of being overthrown. Zeus's mother hid him in Crete, and he later forced Cronus to vomit up his siblings, defeated the Titans and divided the world: Zeus took the sky, Poseidon the sea, Hades the underworld. He ruled from Mount Olympus. His many affairs with goddesses and mortal women produced gods and heroes.

One story matters especially for Acts. The Roman poet Ovid (*Metamorphoses* 8.611-724) tells how Jupiter and Mercury (Zeus and Hermes) once visited the hill country of Phrygia disguised as travellers. Everyone turned them away except an old couple, Baucis and Philemon, who were rewarded while their neighbours were destroyed by a flood. Many commentators think a local version of this legend explains why the Lystrans were so quick to honour Paul and Barnabas: they did not want to make the same mistake twice.
16531:
**Lystra.** After Paul heals a man lame from birth, the crowd shouts in Lycaonian, 'The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!' They call Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, 'because he was the chief speaker'. The priest of Zeus, whose temple stood in front of the city, brings oxen and garlands to the gates (Acts 14:8-13). Paul answers with the first recorded sermon to pure pagans in Acts: turn from 'these vain things' to the living God who made heaven and earth and has shown his goodness through rain and harvests (Acts 14:15-17) — taking for the true God the very gifts Zeus was credited with.

**Ephesus.** The town clerk calls the Artemis statue 'the image which fell down from Jupiter' (Acts 19:35), literally 'fallen from Zeus' or 'from the sky' — probably a meteorite or an object believed to have fallen from heaven.

**Zeus in the temple.** In 167 BC the Seleucid king Antiochus IV rededicated the Jerusalem temple to Zeus Olympios (1 and 2 Maccabees describe this). Many interpreters see this as the 'abomination that makes desolate' of Dan 11:31 and Dan 12:11, which Jesus reapplies to a future crisis (Matt 24:15). The Maccabean link is the majority scholarly view; some conservative readers see Daniel pointing beyond it as well.

**Pergamum.** Jesus tells the church at Pergamum that they live 'where Satan's throne is' (Rev 2:13). The huge Altar of Zeus there is one candidate; others are the imperial cult temple or the healing sanctuary of Asclepius. Debated.

16539: Pergamum's great Altar of Zeus is one possible referent of 'Satan's throne'; scholars also propose the emperor cult or Asclepius. Debated.

16571: Hermes was the Greek messenger god, patron of speech, travel, merchants and tricksters; the Romans called him Mercury. At Lystra the crowd called Paul 'Hermes' because he did most of the talking. One of the Christians Paul greets in Rome is also named Hermes, a common name.
16572: Born in a cave on Mount Cyllene, the baby Hermes crept out on his first day, invented the lyre from a tortoise shell, and stole fifty cattle from his brother Apollo, walking them backwards to confuse the trail. Zeus was amused and made him the herald of the gods. He guided travellers and also led the souls of the dead to Hades. Square pillars with his head and phallus, called herms, stood at crossroads and doorways. As 'Hermes Logios' he was the god of eloquence — which is exactly why the Lystrans gave Paul his name.
16573:
At Lystra the crowd calls Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes 'because he was the chief speaker' (Acts 14:12). The detail shows the crowd's logic: the quieter, perhaps more dignified Barnabas was cast as the chief god, and the talkative Paul as his spokesman. Paul refuses the honour and urges them to turn from these 'vain things' to the living God (Acts 14:15).

In Rom 16:14, Paul greets a believer named Hermes. Names derived from gods were normal in the Roman world and carried no religious meaning in themselves.
16575: Because Paul did the preaching, the people of Lystra identified him with the gods' messenger. Within days, opponents from Antioch and Iconium turned the same crowd to stone him (Acts 14:19).
16577: Among Paul's greetings is a believer called Hermes, a reminder that pagan names were simply names.

16583: In late antiquity Hermes was merged with the Egyptian Thoth as 'Hermes Trismegistus', the supposed author of mystical writings (the Hermetica) that influenced Renaissance thought. The caduceus is still (inaccurately) used as a medical symbol, a confusion with the single-snake rod of Asclepius.

16598: Artemis was the great goddess of Ephesus, and her temple there was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. The Ephesian Artemis was not quite the slim huntress of Greek myth but an older Anatolian mother-goddess. When Paul's preaching hurt the trade in silver shrines, a silversmith named Demetrius started a riot in which a crowd chanted 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!' for two hours.
16599:
In standard Greek myth, Artemis was the virgin huntress, daughter of Zeus and Leto and twin of Apollo, goddess of wild places and of childbirth. The Ephesians claimed she had actually been born near their city, in the grove of Ortygia. Their Artemis blended the Greek goddess with an older Anatolian goddess, which explains her distinctive statue. The many rounded objects on her chest have been explained as breasts, eggs, bull testicles from sacrifices, or decorative pendants; scholars still debate this.

The temple was rebuilt several times. Herostratus burned it in 356 BC, reportedly to make himself famous, on the night Alexander the Great was said to have been born. The rebuilt temple, about four times the size of the Parthenon, was the one Paul knew.
16600:
Paul spent about two to three years in Ephesus (Acts 19:8-10; Acts 20:31), and so many people abandoned magic that they burned scrolls worth fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:19). Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Artemis, gathered the craftsmen: Paul's message that 'gods made with hands are not gods' threatened both their income and the goddess's honour (Acts 19:24-27). The crowd rushed into the theatre shouting 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!' for about two hours (Acts 19:28-34). The town clerk calmed them by reminding them that Ephesus was the 'temple-keeper' (neokoros) of Artemis, that Paul's companions had neither robbed temples nor blasphemed the goddess, and that the courts were open (Acts 19:35-40).

Some scholars also read parts of 1 Timothy, written to Timothy in Ephesus, against the background of the Artemis cult, especially the reference to women being 'saved through childbearing' (1 Tim 2:15), since Artemis was the protector in childbirth. This is a minority but much-discussed reading; others see no specific link.
16602: An economic and religious protest fills the great theatre of Ephesus. Luke presents it as proof of the gospel's impact: the trade in shrines was suffering.
16603: Ephesus was famous for magic ('Ephesian letters' were protective spells). New believers burn their scrolls publicly.
16605: Some read the instructions about women and childbirth against the local goddess cult; others think the letter addresses general false teaching. See the gender-roles debate.

16609: After six years of searching, Wood found the temple's foundations under deep silt. Only one re-erected column now stands. Hogarth found early foundation deposits including some of the earliest coins ever made.
16612: Two marble copies of the cult statue ('Great Artemis' and 'Beautiful Artemis'), carefully buried in antiquity, show the goddess's distinctive form.

Ephesus later hosted the Council of Ephesus (431), which honoured Mary as Theotokos; some writers claim Marian devotion simply replaced Artemis, but historians see a far more complex history.

16638: Castor and Pollux, the 'Dioscuri', were twin gods who protected sailors. Luke notes that the ship that carried Paul from Malta to Italy had their figure as its emblem. It is a small detail, but a telling one: the prisoner who had just survived shipwreck by trusting God sails on under the badge of the sailors' pagan saviours.
16639: Leda, queen of Sparta, bore twins: Castor, son of her mortal husband Tyndareus, and Pollux (Polydeukes), son of Zeus. When Castor was killed, Pollux begged to share his immortality with his brother, so the two alternated between the underworld and Olympus — or, in another version, became the constellation Gemini. Sailors believed the twins appeared in storms as the electrical glow on masts later called St Elmo's fire, a sign of rescue.
16640: After three months on Malta, Paul and his companions sailed on 'a ship of Alexandria, which had wintered in the isle, whose sign was Castor and Pollux' (Acts 28:11). Grain ships from Alexandria often carried a carved or painted emblem at the bow. Luke's detail reflects eyewitness precision (the passage is one of the 'we' sections), and readers have often noted the irony: the true protector at sea in the previous chapter was the God whose angel promised Paul safety (Acts 27:23-25).

16658: An altar inscribed 'To an unknown god'
16660: When Paul visited Athens he noticed an altar inscribed 'To an unknown god'. He used it as the starting point for his speech to the city's council: 'What you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.' Ancient writers confirm that Athens had altars to 'unknown gods', though no altar with Paul's exact wording has been found.
16661: There was no myth: the unknown god was not a specific deity. Greeks feared offending gods they did not know about. A story told by Diogenes Laertius (*Lives of the Philosophers* 1.110) says that during a plague the seer Epimenides of Crete let sheep wander from the Areopagus and sacrificed wherever they lay down 'to the appropriate god', so that anonymous altars could still be found around Athens. The travel writer Pausanias (*Description of Greece* 1.1.4) mentions altars 'of the gods called unknown' at the Athenian harbour of Phalerum.
16662:
In Athens, Paul is 'provoked' by the many idols (Acts 17:16). Invited to explain his teaching at the Areopagus, he says he saw an altar 'To an unknown god' and announces the God whom they worship in ignorance (Acts 17:22-23). He then explains, without quoting Hebrew Scripture, that this God made the world, does not live in temples, needs nothing, made all nations from one man and set their times and boundaries 'so that they should seek God' (Acts 17:24-27). He quotes Greek poets: 'In him we live and move and have our being' (often attributed to Epimenides) and 'For we are also his offspring' (Aratus, *Phaenomena* 5) (Acts 17:28). He ends with a call to repentance and the resurrection, at which some mock, some want to hear more, and a few believe, including Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris (Acts 17:30-34).

Ancient sources speak of altars to 'unknown gods' in the plural. Jerome (commentary on Titus 1:12) claimed the inscription actually read 'to the gods of Asia, Europe and Africa, to unknown and foreign gods' and that Paul adapted it to the singular. Others think a single altar with a singular inscription is perfectly plausible. Debated.
16664: Paul uses a pagan altar, Greek poets and the shared human search for God to introduce the Creator and the risen Jesus.
